course_title: Foundation of the Science of Learning

learning_outcomes.description: Access, interpret, and critically evaluate scientific articles relevant to science of learning practices and/or research.
Explicate key ideas about the brain and mind, and how function is determined.
Consider, critically evaluate, and implement psychological theories relevant to education and learning.
Describe processes leading to the development of self-regulated learning.
Identify the many factors that affect the dynamic process of development and learning across the lifespan.
Translate key teachings and learnings into each students own personal and professional practice through the development of a personal theory.

assessments.task_description:
Topic: Beliefs about learning

The Aim of the Activity: To reflect on current beliefs about learning and establish a personal foundational theoretical position of how you think people learn.

The Activity: Your personal beliefs about learning shape the way you engage in your own learning experiences or how you might design and deliver learning experiences for others such as your students or colleagues. Drawing on existing theoretical positions, as well as new insights from the Science of Learning, this task invites you to compose a brief personal learning theory which you will build upon as we progress through the course.

Draw on existing theory and literature to reflect on and compose a response to the following questions:

  1. What is your current personal philosophy of learning?
  2. In your response reflect on these sub-questions: What is learning? How do you think people learn?
  3. What experiences, ideas, beliefs, evidence, and existing theories underpin your current philosophy?

assessments.task_description:
Topic: Mobilising knowledge across disciplinary lines

The Aim of the Task:

We live, learn and work in a world that is undergoing rapid and profound transformation. Advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence, increasing flexibility in learning and working arrangements, continuously evolving professional roles and opportunities, blurring of boundaries between work and life, and rising awareness of the importance and impact of professional satisfaction, sense of belonging and wellbeing are reshaping roles, capability demands, and how people experience learning and work (Beier et al., 2025; Cascio, 2019; Osher & Pittman, 2024; Parker & Knight, 2023). Developing our capacity for continuous learning across our life course is now more essential than ever to ensure workforce participation and professional growth (Beier, et al., 2025; Lund et al., 2021).

Drawing on interdisciplinary research, the Science of learning has evidenced that meaningful learning is context-dependent, weaving together knowledge, skill, cognition, emotion, social interaction, lived experience, culture and context (Immordino-Yang, et al., 2024). Learning also develops within a learning ecosystem – recognising the reciprocal influence of individual, interpersonal, social, cultural, political, geographical, historical factors and influences. In ‘Weaving a Colorful Cloth’, Immordino-Yang and colleagues (2024) describe how learning is subjective, shaped by interdependent factors, which they articulate through five interrelated principles. Using the metaphor of weaving, the authors illustrate how, when we learn, multiple ‘threads’ weave together to create a unique autobiographical experience. Autobiographical, meaningful learning involves the active process of “internally focused sense-making and externally focused self-expression and action in the world” (Immordino-Yang et al., 2024, p. 11).

The Task:

In this task, you are to examine your own meaningful learning and how you can foster the capabilities needed for continuous, agile learning. Through deep reflection and critical engagement with the literature and learning theory you will examine your autobiographical learning ecosystem: what has shaped and is shaping you as a learner, what beliefs, values, knowledge, skills, experiences, emotions and relationships support and nurture you as a learner.  Through this reflection and exploration of the literature you will create a portfolio to illustrate how the threads of your unique learning ecosystem contribute to weaving your own ‘colourful cloth’.

  1. Read and reflect on the core reading in relation to yourself as a learner, referencing the key principles in your task (we will also be engaging in multiple activities related to this reading across the semester):
  2. Immordino-Yang, M. H., Nasir, N. S., Cantor, P., & Yoshikawa, H. (2024). Weaving a colorful cloth: Centering education on humans’ emergent developmental potentials. Review of Research in Education, 47(1), 1-45. https://doi.org/10.3102/0091732X231223516(Original work published 2023)
  3. Each week (Weeks 1-9), reflect on the course content, readings, discussions and activities and consider how these ideas inform your understanding of yourself as a continuous learner and how you can use these insights to enhance meaningful learning.

a.     What insights challenge/ affirm/ extend your thinking about meaningful learning?

b.     What do you think has contributed to your ‘colourful cloth’ as a learner? Give examples of your own learning experiences.

c.     What questions or wonderings do these insights raise for you?

d.     Illustrate your thinking, idea generation, reflection, problem solving

3.     Draw on the course readings and additional literature to support your reflections and examination of meaningful learning.

4.     Synthesise your reflections across Weeks 1-9 in a brief summary (approx. 500 words) of what meaningful learning is for you, illustrating the components that are woven together to create your unique colourful cloth.

assessments.task_description:
The multi-disciplinary nature of the science of learning makes the process of mobilising or translating this knowledge into authentic teaching, learning, and training environments a complex and challenging one (see Daniel, 2012; Fischer, 2009; Joram, Gabriele, & Walton, 2020; Lysenko, Abrami, Bernard, Dagenais, & Janosz, 2014; MacMahon, Leggett & Carroll, 2022; van Atteveldt, Tijsma, Janssen, & Kupper, 2019). However, seeking ways to overcome these complexities and challenges has immense value for the field and reciprocal benefits for both educators and researchers (Hobbis et al., 2018). Levin (2013) conceptualised the process of knowledge mobilisation as involving three domains: knowledge production, knowledge use, and knowledge mediation. Knowledge brokers – individuals who can act as a conduit between research and practice – are fundamental to effective knowledge mediation, supporting educators and other users of Science of Learning research to effectively engage with and apply research in contextually relevant ways (Brown, 2020; Cooper et al., 2020; Farley-Ripple, 2017; Gorard et al., 2020; Hobbis et al., 2019; Neal et al., 2015).

You can play an important role in your context as a mediator of the Science of Learning. Through thoughtfully designed professional learning, you can support your colleagues to build their knowledge, capabilities, and efficacy in the Science of Learning and its mobilisation into practice.  

Your final assessment task is to prepare a professional learning presentation that explains and illustrates ways to mobilise a Science of Learning Principle, concept or strategy into your teaching/ learning/ training context. The presentation is to be designed for your colleagues in your professional working context and must feature active learning experiences and key practical applications of the Science of Learning. 

Use the prompts below to guide your presentation.

  • Clearly set the context for your presentation, i.e.: who the audience is – you are to design your presentation for them to actively engage in the learning experience.
  • Clearly articulate and explain your chosen principle, positioning it clearly within the holistic Science of Learning lens and literature.
  • Explain the role of the chosen principle in the learning process relevant to your identified audience, synthesising and clearly communicating the key research supporting this principle in a way that is accessible, relevant and meaningful for this audience.
  • Provide clear illustrations of how this principle can be applied into practice in your audience’s context, directly engaging the participants in activities and/ or strategies that reflect your chosen principles. 
  • Innately demonstrate your understanding of common mobilisation barriers and design the presentation with strategies for overcoming or reducing these barriers in your context.
  • Demonstrate an understanding of the design principles informed by the Science of Learning through the layout, activities, and presentation of the task (your aim is to engage and inspire your colleagues, and to promote thinking, feeling and learning).

After your presentation, 5 minutes will be allocated, during which time you will be expected to satisfactorily respond to spontaneous and pertinent questions from your peers and lecturer about the content of your presentation, demonstrating your understanding of the Science of Learning principle or concept, the underlying research evidence, and mobilisation considerations.
assessments.submission_guidelines: Your presentation is to be presented in real-time to the lecturer and peers from EDUC7059. It must include some interactive activities and is not to be read from a script or presented as a lecture.

learning_activities.topic:
Week 1 - Introduction to the Science of Learning

The first week of this course will provide an overview of the science of learning. Key questions are explored, such as: What is Learning? What is the Science of Learning? A range of learning theories will be explored and considered. The structure of the course will be outlined and assessment explained.


Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
Week 2 - The Brain, The Mind, The Body

This week we will be looking at some foundational ideas from psychology and neuroscience that inform the Science of Learning. We will explore the varying philosophical foundations of the key disciplines and consider the challenges when merging them together. We will also begin to explore the intersection of brain-body and environment.


Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
Week 3 - Mobilising the SoL into Practice

As a multi-disciplinary field, the science of learning presents complex challenges when we want to mobilise this research into applied settings. In Week 3 we will be taking a critical lens to the Science of Learning and considering some of the challenges and hurdles when translating multidisciplinary research into real-world practice. We will be discussing different models of knowledge mobilisation and reflecting on contextual and methodological challenges when using research to inform practice. We will also explore some frameworks to support effective mobilisation.

Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
Week 4 - Understanding the Conditions for Learning

This week we will begin our look at how we create the conditions for learning, recognising that learning is a complex, embodied process that integrates the brain, body and environment. We will look specifically at the role of emotions in learning and examine a case study of an adolescent learner to unpack the interconnectedness of emotions and cognition.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05

learning_activities.topic:
Week 5 - Understanding the Conditions for Learning

We are social beings who exist in a social world, and who learn, teach, lead, and work in social contexts. This week we will explore how the science of learning is informing our understanding of social connection and the importance of relationships to learning and thriving. We will consider ways we can utilise this knowledge to design more effective learning and teaching experiences across the lifespan.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L04, L05

learning_activities.topic:
Week 6 - Understanding the conditions for learning

Being comfortable with uncertainty – groundwork for deep learning. This week we will delve into what the science says about some important epistemic emotions and higher order thinking processes including curiosity, creativity, interest & confusion, and how we can create the conditions for deep learning. These deep learning constructs are frequently discussed but often misunderstood and underutilised in learning.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
Week 7 - Cognition

This week we will start looking more deeply into some important learning constructs, including attention, memory and executive functions, including theories such as Cognitive Load Theory. We will explore some guiding principles and some evidence-based strategies that have been shown to promote attention, memory and/ or executive functioning skills and will consider how we can apply these into our own learning contexts.

Learning outcomes: L01, L02, L03, L05, L06

learning_activities.topic:
Week 8 - Self-Regulated Learning and Metacognition

Self-Regulated Learning and Effective learning Strategies. The capacity and efficacy to be able to understand, manage, and reflect on one's own thinking, learning, emotions, motivations, and capabilities is a powerful tool for supporting learning, agency, wellbeing and success across the lifespan. However, we often overlook teaching our learners HOW to learn. This week we will explore some theories of self-regulated learning and metacognition, and a range of effective learning strategies to promote SRL.

Learning outcomes: L01, L03, L04, L05

Making sense of the science of learning in our contexts: this week will be a revisiting of key principles and ideas from across the previous weeks and how we can be using these in our diverse contexts and settings to promote learning. The lecture will also be an opportunity to engage in some collaborative peer feedback processes in relation to the assessment 2.

Neurodiversity. The science of learning and related fields are providing important insight into how differences in learner attributes can be better understood and supported. This week we will explore how we might reframe some common developmental differences to promote more positive experiences for neurodiverse learners.
